hints: Picture what the word lattice means for any solid, think about fixed positions repeating in three dimensions rather than random movement.
walkthrough:
Visualise solid iodine at particle level**
At room temperature iodine is a dark grey solid made of discrete $\text{I}_2$ molecules, not single atoms or ions. In the solid state these molecules lose their freedom to move and become locked in fixed positions.

Link lattice to regularity**
A lattice simply means a repeating, ordered framework. So you can describe the solid as $\text{I}_2$ molecules arranged regularly and uniformly throughout, held in place by weak forces between them.
Final answer: The $\text{I}_2$ molecules are held in a regular / uniform arrangement.

hints: Separate your thinking into two scales, what holds the two iodine atoms together inside one $\text{I}_2$ molecule, and what holds one $\text{I}_2$ molecule to its neighbour.
When solid iodine forms purple vapour, the vapour is still $\text{I}_2$ molecules, so decide which type of attraction must stay intact and which must be broken.
walkthrough:
List everything present in the solid**
Inside each $\text{I}_2$ molecule the two iodine atoms share a pair of electrons, that is a strong covalent bond. Between neighbouring $\text{I}_2$ molecules there are only weak temporary induced dipole-dipole forces, also called London dispersion forces. Iodine is non-polar so there is no permanent dipole-dipole or hydrogen bonding.

Decide what heating to vapour does**
Sublimation separates whole $\text{I}_2$ molecules from each other to give gaseous $\text{I}_2$. You are not splitting $\text{I}_2$ into atoms, so the covalent bonds remain untouched. Only the weak London dispersion forces between molecules are overcome.

Final answer: Forces present: covalent bonds (within $\text{I}_2$) AND (temporary) induced dipole-dipole / London dispersion forces (between $\text{I}_2$ molecules).
Forces overcome on heating to vapour: (temporary) induced dipole-dipole / London dispersion forces only.

hints: Focus on the two iodine atoms in the centre that bridge the two Al atoms, and look carefully at the symbols for the shared electrons in the overlap regions.
walkthrough:
Spot how to recognise a dative bond in the dot-cross diagram**
A normal covalent bond shows one cross from one atom and one dot from the other in the overlap. A dative bond shows both electrons coming from the same atom, so you see $\text{x}\text{x}$ or $++$ together in one overlap.

Count them in $\text{Al}_2\text{I}_6$**
The molecule is a dimer with two bridging iodine atoms joining the two Al centres. Each bridging iodine donates one lone pair to form one dative bond to an Al, giving 2 dative bonds in total. The terminal $\text{Al-I}$ bonds are normal covalent bonds.

hints: Recall the definition of a co-ordinate bond, both shared electrons are supplied by one atom to an empty orbital on the other atom.
walkthrough:
Explain the electron source**
Aluminium in $\text{AlI}_3$ is electron deficient with only six electrons in its outer shell. A bridging iodine atom already has full octets and lone pairs available.

Describe the donation**
A lone pair on a bridging iodine is donated into the vacant orbital on Al, forming a shared pair where both electrons originated from iodine. That shared pair is the co-ordinate or dative covalent bond.
Final answer: Iodine atom donates a pair of electrons to form the $\text{Al-I}$ covalent bond.

hints: Write down all four named products first, $\text{H}_2\text{S}$, $\text{S}$, $\text{I}_2$ and $\text{H}_2\text{O}$, alongside the two reactants $\text{HI}$ and $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$.
Use oxidation numbers to see electron change, I goes from -1 to 0 while S goes from +6 down to 0 and -2, then balance atoms so H, S, I and O balance on both sides.
walkthrough:
Assemble the skeleton equation**
Reactants are hydrogen iodide and concentrated sulfuric acid. Products are given as hydrogen sulfide, sulfur, iodine and water:
$$\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 + \text{HI} \rightarrow \text{I}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{H}_2\text{S} + \text{S}$$

Balance with oxidation numbers as a check**
Iodide is a strong reducing agent and reduces $\text{S}(+6)$ in $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ to both $\text{S}(0)$ and $\text{S}(-2)$. Balancing all atoms gives:
$$2\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 + 14\text{HI} \rightarrow 7\text{I}_2 + 8\text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{H}_2\text{S} + \text{S}$$
Check: H 18 each side, S 2 each side, I 14 each side, O 8 each side.

hints: Calculate the oxidation number of iodine in $\text{HI}$ and in $\text{I}_2$, and decide if an increase means oxidation or reduction.
Calculate the oxidation number of sulfur in $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ and in the two sulfur-containing products $\text{S}$ and $\text{H}_2\text{S}$, and decide what a decrease means.
walkthrough:
Track iodine**
In $\text{HI}$, H is +1 so I is $-1$. In $\text{I}_2$, each atom is $0$. The oxidation number rises from $-1$ to $0$, which is loss of electrons, so iodide is oxidised and acts as the reducing agent.

Track sulfur**
In $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$, S is $+6$. In the products S is $0$ in sulfur and $-2$ in $\text{H}_2\text{S}$. The oxidation number falls, which is gain of electrons, so sulfur is reduced and $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ acts as the oxidising agent. Because oxidation and reduction happen together, the reaction is redox.

Final answer: Iodine is oxidised as oxidation number increases from $-1$ in $\text{HI}$ to $0$ in $\text{I}_2$.
Sulfur is reduced as oxidation number decreases from $+6$ in $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ to $0$ in $\text{S}$ OR to $-2$ in $\text{H}_2\text{S}$.
Both oxidation and reduction occur, so redox.
